parts: Communication is the process of sharing facts, ideas, opinions, thoughts and information through speech, writing, gestures or symbols between two or more persons — so it needs at least two persons. Elements of the communication process: sender (source — the person who sends the message), message (the subject matter — facts, ideas, feelings), medium or means (the channel that carries the message — letter, telephone, e-mail), receiver (the person who receives it) and feedback (the receiver's response directed back to the sender). The process is complete only when the receiver understands the message and gives feedback — e.g. drivers stopping at a red light, or a friend nodding.

Communication is to business what the bloodstream is to a person. It expresses facts, figures and ideas; helps control and coordinate departments and motivate employees; links the firm with suppliers and customers; helps the business run efficiently and builds a good public image; educates people and spreads knowledge of new products and techniques; and overcomes barriers of distance and language.

Verbal communication uses words: oral (spoken — talks, meetings, telephone, lectures) or written (letters, memos, circulars, notices, reports). Non-verbal communication: visual — pictures, graphs, symbols, diagrams (a traffic policeman showing a stop sign, a chart in class); aural — sounds such as bells, whistles, sirens (the school bell); gestural — body language (saluting the national flag, nodding, waving, a straight posture showing confidence). In an organisation, formal communication flows through officially prescribed channels; informal communication (the grapevine) flows through personal contacts. Nobody in an organisation can avoid communication.

Letters — written, low cost, keep a record. Telegrams — quick written messages charged by words (now discontinued in India). Telephone — instant oral contact; STD and ISD for distant calls; PABX for offices; mobile phones add SMS (short message service) and MMS. Telex — printed communication by teleprinters connected through an exchange. Fax (facsimile) — instantly sends an exact copy of handwritten or printed matter, diagrams and sketches over telephone lines. E-mail — messages, pictures and files sent instantly over the Internet. Voice mail — a computer system that records and stores telephone messages to be heard later. Teleconferencing — people in different places interact without sitting face to face: audio-conferencing (hear and respond from different locations) and video-conferencing (also see each other).

(1) Badly expressed message — poor words, wrong language, different interpretations (semantic barrier). (2) Screening or filtering — when a message passes through several levels, each person passes on only what suits him, so it gets distorted. (3) Inattention — people do not read notices or listen carefully. (4) Unclarified assumptions — sender and receiver assume different things. (5) Resistance to change — people ignore messages that disturb their routine. (6) Mutual distrust — lack of confidence between superior and subordinates. (7) Status and position — fear stops subordinates from speaking freely. (8) Complex organisation structure — long chains of command break messages down. Noise is any hurdle that disturbs communication.
